explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Isaiah says the mountain of the house of the LORD "…will be established as the chief of the mountains; it will be raised above the hills…" The hills get a front-row seat to look up at it. That's the picture for the last days.

Hidden? Not this mountain. I spent years tucked in the back of a junk drawer, so I know hiding, and this isn't it. The text says it will be "…raised above the hills…" and all nations will stream to it. Nobody streams toward something they can't find.

A mountain sunk below the hills wouldn't be much of a chief, would it? Isaiah says the mountain of the house of the LORD "…will be established as the chief of the mountains; it will be raised above the hills…" That's the opposite of sunk. Up, friend, not down.

I get why you'd think that, since Isaiah is speaking about Judah and Jerusalem. But the text says "…all nations will stream to it." Then it adds that many peoples will come. That's a much bigger crowd than one nation.

That's right. Isaiah says "…all nations will stream to it." Then he says many peoples will come and say, "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD…" (Isa 2:3). That's a much bigger crowd than one nation.
Yes, friend. The peoples say, "He will teach us His ways so that we may walk in His paths." Teaching is what they say He will do for them. That's the answer on the board.
Land isn't what these peoples are asking for. They say the God of Jacob "…will teach us His ways so that we may walk in His paths." They're headed up there to be taught.
Crowns aren't part of what the peoples say. They say the LORD "…will teach us His ways so that we may walk in His paths." Teaching is the thing they name, friend, not a coronation.

True, friend. The verse says, "For the law will go forth from Zion, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem." Zion and Jerusalem both get named right there as where the law and the word go out from. No mystery about the address.
I think that one slipped past you, and that's okay. Isaiah says "…the word of the LORD from Jerusalem." So it's true that the word goes out from there. The law goes out from Zion in the same verse.
That's it. Isaiah says, "They will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks." Swords become plowshares and spears become pruning hooks. Same metal, new job.

Burying them would be tidy, but that's not what the text says. It says, "They will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks." The weapons get reworked into something different.
Trophies would just keep the swords on the wall, friend. Isaiah says the nations "…will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks." They hammer them into something new.

Right. Isaiah says, "Nation will no longer take up the sword against nation, nor train anymore for war." Nation against nation, and no training for war either. That's a quiet day at the practice field.
Harvest sounds like a nice thing to train for, doesn't it? But the verse says "…nor train anymore for war." War is the one they stop practicing.

Travel is close to what the peoples are doing in verse 3, since they're heading up the mountain. But in verse 4 the text says nations will no longer "…train anymore for war." The training they put down is war training.

explanations.answer: Walk in the light of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The prophet says, "Come, O house of Jacob, let us walk in the light of the LORD." It comes right after the picture of the nations streaming to the mountain. Jacob's house gets invited to walk in that light.
No walls are mentioned here. The prophet says, "Come, O house of Jacob, let us walk in the light of the LORD." The invitation is to walk in that light.

I'd love a gift basket moment, but the text doesn't have one. The prophet says, "Come, O house of Jacob, let us walk in the light of the LORD." It's an invitation to walk, and he's including himself with "let us."

explanations.answer: They're filled with influences from the east
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the prophet gives. He says the LORD has abandoned His people "…because they are filled with influences from the east…" It's right there in verse 6. Filled up to the brim, friend.

explanations.answer: They've moved far away from Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Moving day isn't in this verse. The prophet says they've been abandoned "…because they are filled with influences from the east…" Distance from Jerusalem doesn't come up.

The text doesn't say a word about sacrifices here. The reason in verse 6 is that "…they are filled with influences from the east…" When the reason is written down, I'm not going to make up a different one.
True. Verse 7 says, "Their land is full of silver and gold, with no limit to their treasures…" Full is the word. The prophet isn't being shy about it.

Careful, friend, that one's a trap. Verse 7 says, "Their land is full of silver and gold, with no limit to their treasures…" Full, and then "no limit" on top of full. I've never had a cookie jar that full.
Yes, friend. The prophet says, "Their land is full of idols…" Full of silver, full of horses, and full of idols too. The land is packed.
Prophets would have been a nice thing to fill a land with. But verse 8 says, "Their land is full of idols…" That's the third thing on the list.
Soldiers could fit with all those chariots, I'll give you that. But verse 8 says, "Their land is full of idols…" Chariots are in verse 7, and idols are what come next.

I can see why a gentle ending seems likely, but this is a heavy verse. After the idols, it reads, "So mankind is brought low, and man is humbled…" and then it says, "…do not forgive them!" So the prophet doesn't ask for forgiveness here. He says the opposite.
That's right, friend. This is a heavy verse. It says mankind is brought low and man is humbled. Then it says, "…do not forgive them!" No request for forgiveness there.

explanations.answer: In the rocks and the dust
explanations.explanation: Yes. Verse 10 says, "Go into the rocks and hide in the dust from the terror of the LORD and the splendor of His majesty." The hiding spot is rocks and dust. That's not a cozy place.
City walls aren't the hiding spot in this verse. It says, "Go into the rocks and hide in the dust…" The terror of the LORD and the splendor of His majesty are what they're hiding from.

Temple courts, huh? I get it, that's where I'd run too. But the verse sends them somewhere a lot rougher. It says, "Go into the rocks and hide in the dust from the terror of the LORD and the splendor of His majesty." No courtyard, no cushions, nobody bringing you a cookie.
That one goes in the first blank. Verse 11 says, "The proud look of man will be humbled, and the loftiness of men brought low…" It's the proud look that gets lowered.
That's the word for the second blank. The verse says, "the LORD alone will be exalted in that day." Alone, friend. Nobody else is sharing that spot.
Rewarded sounds nice, but it's not in this verse. It says the proud look of man "…will be humbled…" The LORD alone is the one who "…will be exalted in that day."
Spared isn't what the verse says. The proud look of man "…will be humbled…" and "the LORD alone will be exalted in that day." Those are the two words that fit the blanks.

Tested is a decent guess, but the text doesn't use it. Verse 11 says the proud look of man "…will be humbled…" and then, "the LORD alone will be exalted in that day." Humbled and exalted are the two that fit.
Yes. Verse 12 says, "For the Day of the LORD of Hosts will come against all the proud and lofty, against all that is exalted…" Everything that's lifted up gets humbled. It's a day aimed at pride.
That's not who the verse names. It says the Day of the LORD of Hosts "…will come against all the proud and lofty, against all that is exalted…" The poor and the weak aren't on that list.
Far-off nations aren't named in this verse. It says the day "…will come against all the proud and lofty, against all that is exalted…" The target is pride itself, wherever it's found.
That's the word. Verse 18 says, "…and the idols will vanish completely." Gone, friend. Not one left behind.
The idols aren't coming back in this verse. It says, "…and the idols will vanish completely." Vanish is the one that fits the blank.
Rule is a big word, but the idols don't get it. The text says, "…and the idols will vanish completely." That's a pretty different ending from ruling.

An army makes sense as a reason to run. But the text gives a different one. Verse 19 says they flee "…away from the terror of the LORD and from the splendor of His majesty, when He rises to shake the earth." No invading army is mentioned.
That's right, friend. Verse 19 says men flee "…away from the terror of the LORD and from the splendor of His majesty, when He rises to shake the earth." The verse doesn't mention an army at all.

Yes. Verse 20 says men "…cast away to the moles and bats their idols of silver and gold…" Silver and gold idols, tossed to the moles and bats. That's quite a turn for something people once bowed down to.
Lions and bears sound dramatic. But verse 20 says men "…cast away to the moles and bats their idols of silver and gold…" The ones receiving them are small, dark-dwelling creatures.
That's a fun pair, but it's not the one in the verse. Verse 20 says men "…cast away to the moles and bats their idols of silver and gold…" Moles and bats are the ones named.

explanations.answer: He only has breath in his nostrils
explanations.explanation: That's right. Verse 22 says, "Put no more trust in man, who has only the breath in his nostrils." Then it asks, "Of what account is he?" The prophet is saying man isn't the one to lean on.

explanations.answer: He only has dust beneath his feet
explanations.explanation: Dust is nearby in this chapter, since verse 10 mentions hiding in it. But verse 22 describes man as one "…who has only the breath in his nostrils." Breath is the word it uses.

explanations.answer: He only has gold in his hands
explanations.explanation: Gold shows up earlier, in verse 7, where the land is full of silver and gold. But verse 22 describes man as one "…who has only the breath in his nostrils." It's breath, not gold.
